units.passage: Use of SimCheck (or another plagiarism detection service) is entirely in the discretion of the instructor, but use of such services requires
units.policy: Use of SimCheck or another plagiarism detection service is entirely in the discretion of the instructor, but requires advance notice in the syllabus and a signed consent form from each student.
units.why: 'Use of SimCheck ... is entirely in the discretion of the instructor' but needs advance syllabus notice and signed consent. This concerns plagiarism detection, not AI, and no type covers consent to plagiarism tools, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors must give students advance syllabus notice that plagiarism or AI detection services will be used. / Instructors who use SimCheck or other plagiarism detection must give advance syllabus notice and obtain signed student consent (plagiarism tools, not AI-specific).

units.passage: If an instructor chooses to use a generative AI detection tool against University recommendations, it is important to obtain a signed consent before submitting student work to a generative AI detection tool to (a) notify students that you are using the tool, and (b) obtain FERPA consent and copyright permission
units.policy: Before submitting student work to a generative AI detection tool, an instructor obtains a signed consent that notifies students of the tool and provides FERPA consent and copyright permission.
units.why: Instructors who use a detector 'against University recommendations' must 'obtain a signed consent' to notify students and obtain FERPA consent and copyright permission; a consent condition on detection. No type is about student consent to detection tools, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors must notify students and obtain signed FERPA and copyright consent before submitting student work to an AI detection tool. / Instructors must notify students and obtain signed FERPA and copyright consent before uploading their work to AI detection or plagiarism tools.

units.passage: it is important that every researcher consider their use of AI tools carefully to be consistent with their core values.
units.why: "it is important that every researcher consider their use of AI tools carefully to be consistent with their core values" asks for personal reflection on whether to use AI; no existing type covers values-based reflection.
units.uncovered_note: Researchers should consider whether their AI use is consistent with their own core values.

units.passage: Students using AI for a research project, a research manuscript, or creative work must have documented prior approval from their faculty mentor for the project.
units.policy: Students using AI for a research project, a research manuscript, or creative work must have documented prior approval from their faculty mentor for the project.
units.why: Students "must have documented prior approval from their faculty mentor" before using AI; a gate by the mentor that is not a per-instructor default (P04) but a required approval, hence UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Students must obtain documented prior approval from their faculty mentor before using AI in a research project.

units.passage: Label synthetic media and use content provenance measures (e.g., watermarking/metadata) where feasible for generative outputs.
units.why: "Label synthetic media and use content provenance measures (e.g., watermarking/metadata) where feasible for generative outputs" requires generated media to carry labels, which is a rule on marking AI outputs, not on telling someone they are talking to an AI; addressed to all users under the Transparency principle, must.
units.uncovered_note: Generated media must be labeled and carry provenance metadata where feasible (labelling of AI output, not notice of interacting with AI). (Coder A note: Labelling of synthetic media and provenance metadata on generated outputs, not only notice of interacting with an AI system.) (Coder B note: Generated media must be labeled and carry provenance metadata where feasible.)

units.passage: Users must take measures to ensure the security of AI systems, including protecting access to credentials, implementing security patches, and following all laws, regulations, UTRGV policies, UT System requirements, Information Security Office requirements, and industry best practices to prevent unauthorized access or breaches.
units.why: Requires security measures for AI systems (credentials, patches). A security-practice duty not covered by a type about phishing or data privacy, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Coder A: Users must secure AI systems (protect credentials, apply patches, follow security requirements). | Coder B: General security hygiene for AI systems: protect credentials, patch, follow ISO requirements.

units.passage: It is also important to recognize that tools supporting these activities have existed for many years, and concerns related to academic integrity predate Generative AI.
units.why: Frames AI-related integrity worries as continuous with older issues. It sets no rule and fits no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Says similar tools and integrity concerns predate generative AI, normalizing AI as a continuation of existing issues.

units.passage: Using AI tools operated by entities subject to the laws of foreign adversary countries (China, Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Russia, Venezuela) for university work.
units.why: Bans using AI tools operated by entities in listed 'foreign adversary countries' for university work. No type covers a country-based tool ban (P92 is about using approved tools, P65 about review processes), so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Bans AI tools operated by entities in named foreign adversary countries for university work. Prohibits use of AI tools operated by entities in listed foreign adversary countries for university work.

units.passage: Using AI to infer emotional state, affect, or sensitive traits (race, national origin, sex, disability, sexual orientation, religion, political opinion) of students, employees, or applicants. (Grounded in USU's civil-rights obligations under Title VI, Title IX, and the ADA/Section 504; these uses also carry accuracy and bias risks that cannot be adequately mitigated.)
units.why: Prohibits using AI to infer emotional state or sensitive traits of students, employees or applicants. None of the types covers a ban on this kind of inference, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Bans using AI to infer emotion or sensitive traits (race, religion, disability, etc.) of students, employees or applicants. Prohibits using AI to infer emotional state or sensitive personal traits of students, employees or applicants.

units.passage: Collects feedback and provides a path to raise concerns The resource recommendation form and #ai_usu on Slack for general feedback. Individuals affected by an AI-supported decision may raise concerns with the responsible office or the CDPO. GOVERN 5.1 (external feedback); MEASURE 3.3 (feedback and appeal processes)
units.why: The governance table says USU 'collects feedback and provides a path to raise concerns' and that 'Individuals affected by an AI-supported decision may raise concerns with the responsible office or the CDPO'. This is a concern path for affected people, which no existing type names (P54 is policy review, P64 is for students accused of misuse), so UNCOVERED; it permits (may) and is addressed to anyon
units.uncovered_note: People affected by an AI-supported decision may raise concerns with the responsible office or the CDPO (a path to raise concerns and appeal about AI-supported decisions).

units.passage: AI should never be used as a substitute for peer-reviewed research or professional recommendations.
units.why: 'AI should never be used as a substitute for peer-reviewed research or professional recommendations' bars treating AI as a scholarly or expert authority. No existing type names this (P62 governs research venues and funders; P32 is the learner staying the problem-solver), so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: AI is never to be used as a substitute for peer-reviewed research or professional recommendations (bars treating AI as a stand-in for scholarly sources and expert advice, in research and coursework).

units.passage: With recent developments in generative AI capabilities, it is reasonable to be concerned that your students may abuse or misuse these tools to plagiarize, cheat or otherwise violate your standards for academic integrity.
units.why: "it is reasonable to be concerned that your students may abuse or misuse these tools" opens the page by naming the instructor's concern about misuse. It is a rationale (informs, general, instructor) and no existing type describes it: P56 is an institution-wide framework and this sets none.
units.uncovered_note: Frames the guidance by acknowledging instructors' concern that students may misuse generative AI to plagiarize or cheat.

units.passage: If found guilty, the panel will assign penalty based on the following factors: Flagrancy Premeditation Truthfulness
units.why: "the panel will assign penalty based on the following factors: Flagrancy, Premeditation, Truthfulness" says how penalties are set but states no concrete penalty, so not P37; no other type covers the factors for sanctioning.
units.uncovered_note: Penalties are set by the panel according to flagrancy, premeditation and truthfulness, with no fixed sanction named. (Coder B read it as P37: Names factors that determine penalty but states no concrete penalties.)

units.passage: Do you make a distinction between AI assistance and AI text generation?
units.why: 'Do you make a distinction between AI assistance and AI text generation?' is a prompt asking instructors to decide whether to treat assistance and generation differently in their policy. No existing type covers a decision to separate assistance from generation (P18 is prose versus code), so UNCOVERED, as coder B's own fit_note implies.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors decide whether their AI policy separates AI assistance (ideas, feedback, editing) from AI text generation. Coder B coded P18 with the note: question to consider, not a rule; assistance versus generation, not prose versus code.

units.passage: If you wish to use ChatGPT (or other similar tools that generate text) for any part of a graded assignment (from idea generation to text creation to text editing), you must first ask for permission and explain how you plan to use the tool.
units.why: 'you must first ask for permission and explain how you plan to use the tool' requires permission in advance and an explanation of the planned use. No type covers a duty to get prior approval, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Students must obtain the instructor's permission before using AI and explain how they plan to use it. Coder B (coded P10) noted: Prior permission required, not merely asking when unsure.

units.passage: Be aware that any data posted publicly will likely be scraped and used in this way by third parties.
units.why: Notes publicly posted data "will likely be scraped" for AI training and that legality is unresolved; this awareness note fits no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Warns users that data they post publicly is likely to be scraped to train AI models and that the legality is unsettled.

units.passage: While Gen AI provides output to queries, the internal processes it uses to generate content are still unclear.
units.why: "the internal processes it uses to generate content are still unclear" names opacity of AI as a limitation; no type covers transparency of AI systems, so UNCOVERED.
units.fit_note: About transparency of the model's process, not output errors.
units.uncovered_note: Notes that how generative AI produces its answers is opaque, as a limitation to be aware of.

units.passage: Be aware of all that AI can be asked to do. It can condense readings, expand on student writing, translate, edit, adjust tone, imitate other voices, provide content and sources, create images, and more.
units.why: 'Be aware of all that AI can be asked to do. It can condense readings, expand on student writing, translate...' tells instructors to know AI's range of uses before writing a rule; no type captures it.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors should know the full range of tasks AI can perform when drafting their rule.

units.passage: GHS decisions about any potential violation will be based on what guidance faculty provided.
units.why: 'GHS decisions about any potential violation will be based on what guidance faculty provided' makes graduate enforcement depend on the faculty's stated rule; no type covers that.
units.fit_note: Standard is the instructor's guidance, not a type of evidence.
units.uncovered_note: Graduate honor-system outcomes in AI cases depend on the guidance the instructor gave.

units.passage: Document relevant processes in the TrustArc personal data inventory
units.why: Directs users to 'Document relevant processes in the TrustArc personal data inventory', an administrative registration duty that no existing type captures.
units.uncovered_note: Users must register GenAI processes that involve personal data in the university's personal data inventory.

units.passage: However, consider mitigating and aggravating circumstances such as prior conduct history or egregiousness of alleged violation.
units.policy: Faculty consider mitigating and aggravating circumstances, such as prior conduct history or egregiousness of the alleged violation, in determining outcomes.
units.why: Outcomes must consider 'mitigating and aggravating circumstances such as prior conduct history or egregiousness'; no type covers weighing circumstances in sanctions.
units.uncovered_note: When deciding outcomes for misconduct, weigh mitigating and aggravating circumstances such as prior history and how serious the violation is. / Weigh mitigating and aggravating circumstances when deciding sanctions.

units.passage: Maintain confidentiality throughout the process
units.policy: Faculty and staff are encouraged to maintain confidentiality throughout the misconduct process.
units.why: 'Maintain confidentiality throughout the process' is a conduct-process rule that fits no existing type.
units.uncovered_note: Faculty keep misconduct cases confidential throughout the process. / Keep confidentiality during academic misconduct cases.

units.passage: Some responses pointed to the role of faculty mentorship in helping students learn how to use GenAI responsibly, noting that students often take their cues from what instructors do
units.why: 'students often take their cues from what instructors do' says faculty modeling shapes how students use AI. No type covers instructor modeling of AI use, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors' own AI behavior and mentorship shape students' responsible use.

units.passage: Currently, William & Mary does not have a university-wide written policy specifically addressing faculty communication about AI detection or usage policies
units.why: 'William & Mary does not have a university-wide written policy specifically addressing faculty communication about AI detection or usage policies' states that no such policy exists. This is a fact about the policy landscape that matches no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: States that no university-wide written AI policy exists (a gap acknowledgment). / States that no university-wide written policy exists on faculty communication of AI usage or detection policy (a statement of policy absence).

units.passage: Consideration of ways to address questions regarding the ethical use of AI may emerge through the AIIPC in the form of an anonymous ethics portal that responds to inquiries from campus members. An AIIPC Executive Group (a smaller, more operational group of approximately nine members within the AIIPC) will oversee the day-to-day implementation of AI initiatives approved by the entire AIIPC Working Group.
units.why: 'an anonymous ethics portal that responds to inquiries from campus members' proposes a channel for AI ethics questions; not a reporting duty (P71) or training, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: An anonymous portal where campus members can send AI ethics questions to the council. / Proposes an anonymous portal where campus members can ask questions about the ethical use of AI.

units.passage: This framework empowers instructors to shape their pedagogy while upholding academic standards and institutional values. At present, William & Mary has few formal, university-wide policies addressing the use of AI in the classroom.
units.why: 'William & Mary has few formal, university-wide policies addressing the use of AI in the classroom' reports an absence of rules; UNCOVERED (statement of policy status).
units.uncovered_note: States that the university has few formal university-wide AI classroom policies (a statement of the current policy landscape).

units.passage: Like the points raised for teaching, having clarity in understanding about the acceptable uses of AI in research is important. There are currently no policies in place that specifically discuss the use of AI in research .
units.why: 'There are currently no policies in place that specifically discuss the use of AI in research' states that research use is unregulated. As with the earlier gap statement, no type covers it, so UNCOVERED.
units.fit_note: States the absence of a research AI policy rather than a rule.
units.uncovered_note: States that no research AI policy exists (a gap acknowledgment).

units.passage: Formally establish an AI research hub or center that supports interdisciplinary collaboration, coordinates with national initiatives, fosters industry partnerships, and provides centralized resources and strategic guidance
units.why: 'Formally establish an AI research hub or center' is an investment recommendation about research infrastructure. It is not a use rule and fits no type, so UNCOVERED.
units.uncovered_note: Recommends building an AI research center and incentives (seed grants, fellowships); about research capacity, not AI-use rules.
